claim: Circadian rhythms are maintained by a cell-autonomous, transcriptional–translational feedback loop known as the molecular clock.
source: Circadian rhythms are maintained by a cell-autonomous, transcriptional–translational feedback loop known as the molecular clock.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian rhythms and the molecular clock mechanism.

claim: Knocking out skeletal muscle clock function alters titin isoform expression in iMSBmal1-/- mice.
source: Utilizing inducible, skeletal muscle specific, Bmal1 knockout (iMSBmal1-/-) mice, we showed that knocking out skeletal muscle clock function alters titin isoform expression using RNAseq, liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry, and sodium dodecyl sulfate-vertical agarose gel electrophoresis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNAseq, LC-MS, and SDS-VAGE experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Alteration in titin's spring length resulted in sarcomere length heterogeneity in iMSBmal1-/- mice.
source: This alteration in titin's spring length resulted in sarcomere length heterogeneity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of sarcomere length variability shown in the manuscript.

claim: The skeletal muscle clock regulates titin isoform expression through transcriptional regulation of Rbm20.
source: We identified a mechanism whereby the skeletal muscle clock regulates titin isoform expression through transcriptional regulation of Rbm20, a potent splicing regulator of titin.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data, luciferase assays, and expression analyses showing BMAL1/CLOCK regulation of Rbm20.

claim: Environmental circadian rhythm disruption causes significant downregulation of Rbm20 expression.
source: Lastly, we used an environmental model of circadian rhythm disruption and identified significant downregulation of Rbm20 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data from the chronic phase advance (CPA) model showing reduced Rbm20 expression.

claim: Circadian rhythms are intrinsically directed patterns seen in behavior and biology with an ~24 hr periodicity.
source: Circadian rhythms are intrinsically directed patterns seen in behavior and biology with an ~24 hr periodicity (Bass and Takahashi, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bass and Takahashi, 2010.

claim: The molecular clock exists in virtually every cell in the body.
source: The molecular clock exists in virtually every cell in the body and functions to support homeostasis through regulating a daily pattern of gene expression (Merrow et al., 2005; Yoo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Merrow et al., 2005 and Yoo et al., 2004.

claim: BMAL1 is a PAS/basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factor.
source: BMAL1 is a PAS/basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factor that acts as the only nonredundant component of the core clock mechanism (Bunger et al., 2000; Hogenesch et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMAL1 structure supported by citations.

claim: BMAL1 acts as the only nonredundant component of the core clock mechanism.
source: BMAL1 is a PAS/basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factor that acts as the only nonredundant component of the core clock mechanism (Bunger et al., 2000; Hogenesch et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bunger et al., 2000 and Hogenesch et al., 1998.

claim: BMAL1 and CLOCK are transcriptional regulators of both rhythmic and nonrhythmic genes important for cell-type-specific functions.
source: Beyond its role in cellular time keeping, BMAL1 and its partner, CLOCK, have been described as transcriptional regulators of both rhythmic and nonrhythmic genes important for cell-type-specific functions (Bass and Takahashi, 2010; Bozek et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bass and Takahashi, 2010; Bozek et al., 2009; and Miller et al., 2007.

claim: The circadian clock regulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism in skeletal muscle.
source: The most well-studied aspect of these functions, particularly in the context of skeletal muscle, is the circadian clock regulation of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism (Reinke and Asher, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinke and Asher, 2019.

claim: The skeletal muscle clock maintains skeletal muscle structure and function.
source: Our lab has provided evidence suggesting a more expansive role for the skeletal muscle clock through maintenance of skeletal muscle structure and function (McCarthy et al., 2007; Andrews et al., 2010; Schroder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Expression of Myod1 and genes encoding contractile proteins are circadian in the hindlimb muscles of C57BL/6J mice.
source: The first evidence for this role came from microarray analyses showing expression of the myogenic regulatory factor Myod1 as well as genes encoding contractile proteins are circadian in the hindlimb muscles of C57BL/6J mice (McCarthy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCarthy et al., 2007.

claim: Bmal1 knockout mice show diminished force output in whole-muscle and single-fiber mechanics.
source: The molecular clock's proposed role in maintaining muscle function was supported with whole-muscle and single-fiber mechanics data from the Bmal1 knockout mice (Andrews et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andrews et al., 2010.

claim: Bmal1 knockout mice exhibit sarcomere irregularities consistent with diminished force output.
source: Additionally, electron microscopy studies demonstrated sarcomere irregularities consistent with the diminished force output findings.
evidence: This is supported by inference from electron microscopy studies mentioned in the text.

claim: Systemic Bmal1 KO mice exhibit significant behavioral abnormalities.
source: However, these experiments were performed in systemic Bmal1 KO mice that exhibit significant behavioral abnormalities, thus, distinguishing the role of skeletal muscle molecular clock from activity patterns requires further study using more refined approaches and animal models.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the systemic Bmal1 KO model.

claim: Titin is the largest known protein.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and spans the length of the half-sarcomere, from Z-line to M-line, functioning as the structural backbone for the sarcomere and aiding in both active and passive force generation (Freundt and Linke, 2019; Brynnel et al., 2018; Mijailovich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about titin supported by citations.

claim: Titin spans the length of the half-sarcomere, from Z-line to M-line.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and spans the length of the half-sarcomere, from Z-line to M-line, functioning as the structural backbone for the sarcomere and aiding in both active and passive force generation (Freundt and Linke, 2019; Brynnel et al., 2018; Mijailovich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about titin structure supported by citations.

claim: Titin functions as the structural backbone for the sarcomere.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and spans the length of the half-sarcomere, from Z-line to M-line, functioning as the structural backbone for the sarcomere and aiding in both active and passive force generation (Freundt and Linke, 2019; Brynnel et al., 2018; Mijailovich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about titin function supported by citations.

claim: Titin aids in both active and passive force generation.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and spans the length of the half-sarcomere, from Z-line to M-line, functioning as the structural backbone for the sarcomere and aiding in both active and passive force generation (Freundt and Linke, 2019; Brynnel et al., 2018; Mijailovich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about titin function supported by citations.

claim: The I-band region of titin connects the thick filament to the thin filament and acts as a viscoelastic spring.
source: The I-band region of titin connects the thick filament to the thin filament and acts as a viscoelastic spring.
evidence: This is established knowledge about titin structure and function.

claim: The I-band region of titin is primarily composed of immunoglobulin-like (Ig) repeats and the PEVK region.
source: This region is primarily composed of immunoglobulin-like (Ig) repeats and the PEVK region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about titin structure.

claim: Titin undergoes a remarkable amount of splicing within the I-band region.
source: Titin undergoes a remarkable amount of splicing within this region with inclusion or exclusion of these repeats yielding longer or shorter titin proteins, respectively (Guo et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Guo et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012; and Li et al., 2013.

claim: Inclusion or exclusion of Ig repeats yields longer or shorter titin proteins, respectively.
source: Titin undergoes a remarkable amount of splicing within this region with inclusion or exclusion of these repeats yielding longer or shorter titin proteins, respectively (Guo et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Maintenance of titin splicing and isoform composition is needed to maintain muscle function.
source: Maintenance of titin splicing, and thus the isoform composition, is needed to maintain muscle function.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: iMSBmal1-/- mice display muscle weakness defined by ex vivo measures of maximum isometric tetanic force.
source: Importantly, these mice display muscle weakness defined by ex vivo measures of maximum isometric tetanic force (i.e., specific force) (Schroder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schroder et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of Bmal1 in adult skeletal muscle alters splicing in titin's spring region.
source: We show that loss of Bmal1 specifically in adult skeletal muscle alters splicing in titin's spring region, resulting in sarcomere length disruption.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Bmal1 in adult skeletal muscle results in sarcomere length disruption.
source: We show that loss of Bmal1 specifically in adult skeletal muscle alters splicing in titin's spring region, resulting in sarcomere length disruption.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing sarcomere length heterogeneity.

claim: Exon-specific protein changes in titin were identified using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS).
source: Consistent with changes in splicing, we identify exon-specific protein changes in titin using a methodological approach for analyzing titin isoforms using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The skeletal muscle molecular clock regulates Rbm20.
source: Mechanistically, the skeletal muscle molecular clock regulates Rbm20, the gene encoding an RNA-binding protein known to regulate titin splicing.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq, ChIP-PCR, and luciferase assay data.

claim: RBM20 is an RNA-binding protein known to regulate titin splicing.
source: Mechanistically, the skeletal muscle molecular clock regulates Rbm20, the gene encoding an RNA-binding protein known to regulate titin splicing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBM20 function.

claim: Overexpressing RBM20 in iMSBmal1-/- skeletal muscle is sufficient to restore titin isoform expression.
source: Overexpressing RBM20 in iMSBmal1-/- skeletal muscle is sufficient to restore titin isoform expression.
evidence: This is supported by AAV-mediated RBM20 overexpression experiments showing partial restoration of titin isoform.

claim: A chronic jet-lag model with wildtype mice confirms that circadian disruption is sufficient to change Rbm20 expression.
source: Use of a chronic jet-lag model with wildtype mice confirms that circadian disruption is sufficient to change Rbm20 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data from the chronic phase advance (CPA) model.

claim: There is a shift in titin isoform composition in iMSBmal1-/- tibialis anterior muscle from a short isoform to a mixture of both short and long titin proteins.
source: The shift in titin isoforms changes the predominant form from a short isoform to a mixture of both short and long titin proteins.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-VAGE data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: There is no change in total titin expression in iMSBmal1-/- muscle.
source: Using sodium dodecyl sulfate-vertical agarose gel electrophoresis (SDS-VAGE) to analyze gross size changes in titin protein of iMSBmal1-/- tibialis anterior (TA) muscle, we found a shift in titin isoform composition (p<0.01; Figure 1A and B) with no change in total titin expression.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-VAGE data.

claim: iMSBmal1-/- TA muscle showed increased percent spliced in (PSI) of exons 52–88 of the titin transcript compared to iMSBmal1+/+ control samples.
source: iMSBmal1-/- TA muscle showed increased percent sliced in (PSI) of exons 52–88 of the titin transcript compared to iMSBmal1+/+ control samples (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exons 52–88 code for a portion of titin's proximal Ig segment.
source: These exons code for a portion of titin's proximal Ig segment, one of titin's extensible segments within its spring region.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of titin structure and the location of these exons.

claim: Inclusion of exons 52–69, 70–79, and 80–88 was significantly greater in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle.
source: In each of these smaller events, inclusion of exons was significantly greater in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle (Figure 1D; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Peptides representing exons 52–69 were not detected in iMSBmal1+/+ muscle and only identified in the iMSBmal1-/- muscle samples.
source: We then analyzed differential expression of peptides and identified that those representing exons 52–69 were not detected in iMSBmal1+/+ muscle and only identified in the iMSBmal1-/- muscle samples.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The abundance of peptides from exons 70–79 and 80–88 were 18% and 16% greater in the iMSBmal1-/- compared to the iMSBmal1+/+ muscle samples, respectively.
source: The abundance of peptides from the translation of exons 70–79 and 80–88 were 18 and 16% greater in the iMSBmal1-/- compared to the iMSBmal1+/+ muscle samples, respectively (p<0.05; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A total of 1218 peptides corresponding to the Ensembl ENSMUST00000099981.10 titin transcript were identified in the LC-MS analysis.
source: A total of 1218 peptides corresponding to the Ensembl ENSMUST00000099981.10 titin transcript were identified in the LC-MS analysis of which 1009 met our minimum threshold for quantification and were used to calculate exon-specific peptide abundance.
evidence: This is a direct report of the LC-MS experimental results.

claim: 1009 peptides met the minimum threshold for quantification and were used to calculate exon-specific peptide abundance.
source: A total of 1218 peptides corresponding to the Ensembl ENSMUST00000099981.10 titin transcript were identified in the LC-MS analysis of which 1009 met our minimum threshold for quantification and were used to calculate exon-specific peptide abundance.
evidence: This is a direct report of the LC-MS experimental results.

claim: The quantified peptides corresponded to 225 of the 363 known exons in the Ttn gene.
source: These peptides corresponded to 225 of the 363 known exons in the Ttn gene (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the LC-MS experimental results.

claim: Mean sarcomere length did not significantly change following skeletal muscle-specific loss of Bmal1.
source: Using this approach, mean sarcomere length did not significantly change following skeletal muscle-specific loss of Bmal1 (p=0.86; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sarcomere length was significantly more variable in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle.
source: However, sarcomere length homogeneity is a feature of healthy striated muscle, and we noted that sarcomere length was significantly more variable in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle (F = 22.12, p<0.05; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sarcomere length homogeneity is a feature of healthy striated muscle.
source: However, sarcomere length homogeneity is a feature of healthy striated muscle, and we noted that sarcomere length was significantly more variable in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle (F = 22.12, p<0.05; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about muscle structure.

claim: iMSBmal1+/+ muscle had sarcomere lengths of 2.12 ± 0.01 µm while iMSBmal1-/- muscle had sarcomere lengths of 2.28 ± 0.02 µm in epitope-specific antibody measurements.
source: iMSBmal1+/+ muscle had sarcomere lengths of 2.12 ± 0.01 µm while iMSBmal1-/- muscle had sarcomere lengths of 2.28 ± 0.02 µm (F = 3.62, p<0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data using titin epitope-specific antibodies shown in Figure 3D.

claim: iMSBmal1-/- had significantly longer proximal Ig domain lengths (229.5 ± 1.357 nm) than iMSBmal1+/+ samples (182.4 ± 1.388 nm).
source: iMSBmal1-/- had significantly longer proximal Ig domain lengths (229.5 ± 1.357 nm) than the proximal Ig domain from iMSBmal1+/+ samples (182.4 ± 1.388 nm; p<0.0001; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data measuring the distance between Z1Z2 and N2A epitopes shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The difference in proximal Ig domain lengths accounts for the difference in sarcomere lengths.
source: This difference in lengths accounts for the difference we see in sarcomere lengths in these samples.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between proximal Ig domain length and sarcomere length measurements.

claim: The variation around the mean for proximal Ig domain length was not significantly different between iMSBmal1-/- and iMSBmal1+/+ muscle.
source: However, the variation around the mean for proximal Ig domain length was not significantly different (F = 1.338, p=0.12).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the proximal Ig domain length data.

claim: Control eGFP-ACTN2-C2C12 myotubes had an average sarcomere length of 2.756 ± 0.0495 µm.
source: While control myotubes had an average sarcomere length of 2.756 ± 0.0495 µm, Ttn-U7 transfected myotubes had significantly shorter sarcomeres with an average sarcomere length of 2.387 ± 0.0347 µm (p<0.0001, n = 100–200 sarcomeres/two biological replicates; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data from C2C12 myotubes shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ttn-U7 transfected myotubes had significantly shorter sarcomeres with an average sarcomere length of 2.387 ± 0.0347 µm.
source: While control myotubes had an average sarcomere length of 2.756 ± 0.0495 µm, Ttn-U7 transfected myotubes had significantly shorter sarcomeres with an average sarcomere length of 2.387 ± 0.0347 µm (p<0.0001, n = 100–200 sarcomeres/two biological replicates; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data from C2C12 myotubes shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ttn-U7 transfected myotubes had a proximal Ig length of 285.1 ± 3.131 nm compared to 448.0 ± 3.368 nm of control myotubes.
source: Proximal Ig domain lengths were also significantly different. Ttn-U7 transfected myotubes had a proximal Ig length of 285.1 ± 3.131 nm compared to 448.0 ± 3.368 nm of control myotubes (p<0.0001; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data from C2C12 myotubes shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Altering the length of titin's proximal Ig domain causes a change in sarcomere length in skeletal muscle myotubes.
source: These results confirm that altering the length of titin's proximal Ig domain causes a change in sarcomere length in skeletal muscle myotubes.
evidence: This is supported by the U7 snRNP experiments showing that truncating the proximal Ig domain results in shorter sarcomeres.

claim: RBM20 is a well-characterized splicing factor known to target titin pre-mRNA.
source: RBM20 is a well-characterized splicing factor known to target titin pre-mRNA (Guo et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013; Maatz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Guo et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013; and Maatz et al., 2014.

claim: RBM20 is an RNA-binding protein that acts as a splicing repressor.
source: RBM20 is an RNA-binding protein that acts as a splicing repressor such that when present at high levels it binds along titin pre-mRNA preventing normal intronic splicing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBM20 function.

claim: When RBM20 is bound at high levels, titin pre-mRNA undergoes large exon-skipping events.
source: When bound by many RBM20 proteins, titin pre-mRNA undergoes large exon-skipping events whereby the resultant, processed mRNA is shorter than if RBM20 was not present.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBM20 mechanism of action.

claim: Rbm20 mRNA expression was reduced by 34% in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle.
source: Rbm20 mRNA expression was reduced by 34% in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle (p<0.05; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RBM20 protein content decreased by 46% in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle.
source: This reduced expression was also present at the protein level where RBM20 protein content decreased by 46% compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle (p<0.05; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BMAL1, CLOCK, and MYOD1 bind to a common region within intron 1 of Rbm20.
source: As seen in Figure 5C, we detected significant binding of BMAL1, CLOCK, and MYOD1 within a common region of intron 1 of Rbm20.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The binding region in Rbm20 intron 1 contains a putative regulatory element as defined by the third phase of the ENCODE project.
source: Analysis of this region identified a putative regulatory element as defined by the third phase of the ENCODE project (Moore et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by reference to ENCODE data and citation to Moore et al., 2020.

claim: ChIP-PCR confirmed significant binding of BMAL1, CLOCK, and MYOD1 at the Rbm20 intron 1 site.
source: We identified significant binding of BMAL1 (p<0.01), CLOCK (p<0.001), and MYOD1 (p<0.001; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Overexpression of the clock factors in E-Rbm20-Luc transfected myotubes resulted in a 255-fold increase in luciferase activity compared to empty vector control transfected myotubes.
source: We found that overexpression of the clock factors in E-Rbm20-Luc transfected myotubes resulted in a 255-fold increase in luciferase activity compared to empty vector control transfected myotubes (n = 3, p<0.0001, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by dual-luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The increase in luciferase activity with E-Rbm20-Luc is 9.8-fold higher than the increase seen with Rbm20-P-Luc, which lacks the enhancer element.
source: Importantly, this increase is 9.8-fold higher than the increase seen in myotubes transfected with Rbm20-P-Luc, which lacks the enhancer element (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by dual-luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Rbm20 mRNA exhibits a significant difference in expression in the quadriceps muscles under normal light:dark conditions.
source: In Figure 5D, we found that Rbm20 mRNA did exhibit a significant difference in expression in the quadriceps muscles under normal light:dark conditions.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data from the CPA model shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Muscles from the CPA mice exhibit depressed expression of Rbm20, mostly notably at CT30.
source: In contrast, muscles from the CPA mice exhibit depressed expression of Rbm20, mostly notably at CT30, during the subjective rest phase for the mice.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data from the CPA model shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TA muscle from CPA mice showed reduced Rbm20 expression at both time points, but this change was not significant.
source: The results for the TA muscle from the same mice follow a similar trend with reduced Rbm20 expression at both time points in the CPA group, but this change was not significant (p=0.09).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data from the CPA model shown in Figure 5E.

claim: RBM20 protein levels decreased by 38% in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle injected with GFP-AAV.
source: Consistent with our prior measures, RBM20 protein levels decreased by 38% in iMSBmal1-/- muscle compared to iMSBmal1+/+ muscle injected with GFP-AAV (p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Injection of RBM20-AAV into iMSBmal1-/- muscle increased Rbm20 gene expression by 2.8-fold.
source: Injection of RBM20-AAV into iMSBmal1-/- muscle increased Rbm20 gene expression by 2.8-fold (padj<0.05) and RBM20 protein expression almost 2-fold above iMSBmal1+/+-GFP-AAV levels (p<0.05; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq and Western blot data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Injection of RBM20-AAV into iMSBmal1-/- muscle increased RBM20 protein expression almost 2-fold above iMSBmal1+/+-GFP-AAV levels.
source: Injection of RBM20-AAV into iMSBmal1-/- muscle increased Rbm20 gene expression by 2.8-fold (padj<0.05) and RBM20 protein expression almost 2-fold above iMSBmal1+/+-GFP-AAV levels (p<0.05; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of muscle Bmal1 resulted in a significant increase in the long form of titin.
source: Consistent with earlier work, loss of muscle Bmal1 resulted in a significant increase in the long form of titin (p<0.01; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-VAGE data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AAV expression of RBM20 in the iMSBmal1-/- muscle was sufficient to significantly reduce the amount of the long titin isoform to levels closer to wildtype.
source: AAV expression of RBM20 in the iMSBmal1-/- muscle was sufficient to significantly reduce the amount of the long titin isoform to levels closer to wildtype (p<0.05; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-VAGE data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: iMSBmal1-/--RBM20 muscle showed decreased expression of exons 70–88 of titin compared to iMSBmal1-/--GFP muscle.
source: iMSBmal1-/--RBM20 muscle showed decreased expression of exons 70–88 of titin compared to iMSBmal1-/--GFP muscle (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Exons 52–69 showed only a modest increase in expression in muscle-overexpressing RBM20.
source: We did note, however, that exons 52–69 showed only a modest increase in expression in muscle-overexpressing RBM20.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LC-MS confirmed a significant decrease in exons 70–79 inclusion in iMSBmal1-/--RBM20-AAV TA muscle.
source: These changes were confirmed using LC-MS with a significant decrease in exons 70–79 (p<0.001) and 80–88 (p<0.01) inclusion in iMSBmal1-/--RBM20-AAV TA muscle with no significant different in inclusion of exons 52–69 in titin protein (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: LC-MS confirmed a significant decrease in exons 80–88 inclusion in iMSBmal1-/--RBM20-AAV TA muscle.
source: These changes were confirmed using LC-MS with a significant decrease in exons 70–79 (p<0.001) and 80–88 (p<0.01) inclusion in iMSBmal1-/--RBM20-AAV TA muscle with no significant different in inclusion of exons 52–69 in titin protein (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was no significant difference in inclusion of exons 52–69 in titin protein in iMSBmal1-/--RBM20-AAV TA muscle.
source: These changes were confirmed using LC-MS with a significant decrease in exons 70–79 (p<0.001) and 80–88 (p<0.01) inclusion in iMSBmal1-/--RBM20-AAV TA muscle with no significant different in inclusion of exons 52–69 in titin protein (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from the AAV rescue experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: RBM20 rescue with rescue of TTN-splicing resulted in a reduced distance of the PEVK domain from the Z-disc.
source: Longitudinal sections were labeled for these two epitopes (α-actinin/TTN-PEVK) demonstrated that RBM20 rescue with rescue of TTN-splicing resulted in a reduced distance of the PEVK domain from the Z-disc, consistent with a smaller titin isoform within the sarcomere (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduced distance of the PEVK domain from the Z-disc is consistent with a smaller titin isoform within the sarcomere.
source: Longitudinal sections were labeled for these two epitopes (α-actinin/TTN-PEVK) demonstrated that RBM20 rescue with rescue of TTN-splicing resulted in a reduced distance of the PEVK domain from the Z-disc, consistent with a smaller titin isoform within the sarcomere (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between PEVK position and titin isoform size.

claim: MYOD1 works with BMAL1::CLOCK to cooperatively regulate skeletal muscle-specific, clock-controlled genes.
source: The novel link between the muscle circadian clock and RBM20 is of particular importance as our lab recently proposed a mechanism whereby MYOD1 works with BMAL1::CLOCK to cooperatively regulate skeletal muscle-specific, clock-controlled genes (Hodge et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodge et al., 2019.

claim: Rbm20 is a bona fide clock-controlled gene in skeletal muscle.
source: These data confirm that Rbm20 is a bona fide clock-controlled gene in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq, ChIP-PCR, and luciferase data showing clock factor regulation of Rbm20.

claim: Changes to the proximal Ig segment of titin's spring region can alter sarcomere length.
source: We provide direct evidence that changes to the proximal Ig segment of titin's spring region can alter sarcomere length and further support titin's role as a molecular ruler.
evidence: This is supported by the U7 snRNP experiments showing that truncating the proximal Ig domain results in shorter sarcomeres.

claim: RBM20 is a key mediator of titin splicing downstream of the circadian clock.
source: Further, we provide gain of function transcriptome and proteome data, which confirm that RBM20 is a key mediator of titin splicing downstream of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is supported by the AAV-RBM20 rescue experiments showing restoration of titin splicing.

claim: Circadian rhythms are important for maintaining muscle structural integrity.
source: Our findings expand upon the importance of the molecular clock in maintaining skeletal muscle health by showing that circadian rhythms are not only important for the metabolic function but are also important for maintaining muscle structural integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings showing that loss of Bmal1 alters titin splicing and sarcomere structure.

claim: RBM20 is predominantly expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscles.
source: RBM20 is predominantly expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBM20 expression patterns.

claim: Most RBM20 research has been in cardiac muscle as RBM20 mutations are linked to cardiomyopathies.
source: Because most RBM20 research has been in cardiac muscle as RBM20 mutations are linked to cardiomyopathies (Guo et al., 2010), understanding of its role in skeletal muscle remains limited (Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2010.

claim: Understanding of RBM20's role in skeletal muscle remains limited.
source: Because most RBM20 research has been in cardiac muscle as RBM20 mutations are linked to cardiomyopathies (Guo et al., 2010), understanding of its role in skeletal muscle remains limited (Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2010 and general knowledge of the field.

claim: The enhancer region of Rbm20 intron 1 is highly conserved and is maintained in the human ENCODE database of putative enhancers (E1499168).
source: This region of the Rbm20 gene is highly conserved and is maintained in the human ENCODE database of putative enhancers (E1499168).
evidence: This is supported by reference to the ENCODE database.

claim: RBM20 is currently linked to splicing of up to 18 mRNAs in the heart.
source: It is also important to note that RBM20 is currently linked to splicing of up to 18 mRNAs in the heart (Maatz et al., 2014), 5 of which have significant changes in exon inclusion in our model.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maatz et al., 2014.

claim: 5 of the 18 mRNAs spliced by RBM20 in the heart have significant changes in exon inclusion in the iMSBmal1-/- model.
source: It is also important to note that RBM20 is currently linked to splicing of up to 18 mRNAs in the heart (Maatz et al., 2014), 5 of which have significant changes in exon inclusion in our model.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the RNAseq data from the iMSBmal1-/- model.

claim: Regulation of RBM20 downstream of the circadian clocks could contribute to other aspects of muscle structure and function independent of titin splicing.
source: Thus, regulation of RBM20 downstream of the circadian clocks could contribute to other aspects of muscle structure and function independent of titin splicing.
evidence: This is speculation based on the finding that RBM20 regulates multiple mRNAs.

claim: There is a lack of overlap between the RBM20-dependent splicing changes in the heart and the iMSBmal1-/- skeletal muscle model.
source: It is important to note that there is a lack of overlap between the RBM20-dependent splicing changes in the heart and our model in skeletal muscle, suggesting that RBM20 may have tissue-specific targets.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the RNAseq data with published cardiac data.

claim: RBM20 may have tissue-specific targets.
source: It is important to note that there is a lack of overlap between the RBM20-dependent splicing changes in the heart and our model in skeletal muscle, suggesting that RBM20 may have tissue-specific targets.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between cardiac and skeletal muscle.

claim: Circadian rhythm disruption occurs in aging and many chronic diseases.
source: Since circadian rhythm disruption occurs in aging and many chronic diseases, our findings suggest RBM20 and titin splicing could play a broader role in conditions with known muscle weakness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian rhythm disruption in disease.

claim: RBM20 and titin splicing could play a broader role in conditions with known muscle weakness.
source: Since circadian rhythm disruption occurs in aging and many chronic diseases, our findings suggest RBM20 and titin splicing could play a broader role in conditions with known muscle weakness.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings linking circadian disruption to RBM20 and titin splicing.

claim: Maintaining muscle strength in chronic disease states and aging is a strong predictor of mortality.
source: Defining mechanisms to preserve muscle function is important due to the emerging recognition that maintaining muscle strength in chronic disease states and aging is a strong predictor of mortality (Newman et al., 2006; García-Hermoso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newman et al., 2006 and García-Hermoso et al., 2018.

claim: Skeletal muscle function is tightly linked to its structure.
source: Since skeletal muscle function is tightly linked to its structure, we investigated a mechanism that links the molecular clock to sarcomere organization in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is established knowledge in muscle physiology.

claim: Heterogeneous sarcomere lengths would be disadvantageous at the muscle tissue level as the likelihood that an individual sarcomere would be operating at its optimal length is reduced.
source: Heterogeneous sarcomere lengths would be disadvantageous at the muscle tissue level as the likelihood that an individual sarcomere would be operating at its optimal length is reduced (Hou, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hou, 2018.

claim: When the number of crossbridges between the thin and thick filaments is reduced, the maximum force produced by the muscle is diminished.
source: While a sarcomere can generate force outside of optimal length, it is well established that when the number of crossbridges between the thin and thick filaments is reduced, the maximum force produced by the muscle is diminished (Patel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Patel et al., 2004.

claim: Changes to overall titin isoform in skeletal muscle result in changes to the number of serial sarcomeres in an apparent effort to reduce the working range of the sarcomere.
source: Additionally, emerging data suggests that changes to overall titin isoform in skeletal muscle result in changes to the number of serial sarcomeres in an apparent effort to reduce the working range of the sarcomere, with functional consequences.
evidence: This is emerging knowledge in the field.

claim: This study is the first to provide direct correlations between titin exon splicing at the RNA level with peptide expression at the protein level.
source: To our knowledge, we are the first group to provide direct correlations between titin exon splicing at the RNA level with peptide expression at the protein level for the giant protein.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the methodological approach.

claim: Analysis of titin protein isoforms has historically required the use of vertical agarose gels and antibodies that detect repetitive elements to semi-quantitatively measure changes in alternative splicing.
source: Notably, analysis of titin protein isoforms has historically required the use of vertical agarose gels and antibodies that detect repetitive elements to semi-quantitatively measure changes in alternative splicing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about historical methods for analyzing titin.

claim: LC-MS can be used to confirm changes in titin splicing in conditions where titin splicing is disrupted.
source: Our methodology could be used to confirm changes in other conditions where titin splicing is disrupted.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader applicability of the LC-MS method.

claim: Estimations of titin turnover have been measured on the order of days.
source: Estimations of titin turnover have been measured on the order of days, much longer than processes that would predictably be regulated daily by the circadian clock (Isaacs et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Isaacs et al., 1989.

claim: Studies in cardiomyocytes suggest that sarcomeric titin exhibits dynamic exchange within ~14 hr independent of protein turnover.
source: However, studies in cardiomyocytes suggest that sarcomeric titin exhibits dynamic exchange within ~14 hr independent of protein turnover (da Silva Lopes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to da Silva Lopes et al., 2011.

claim: If dynamic titin exchange exists in skeletal muscle, this would allow the fiber to modulate titin length on a more frequent, potentially daily basis.
source: If such a mechanism exists in skeletal muscle, this would allow the fiber to modulate titin length on a more frequent, potentially daily basis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cardiomyocyte data.

claim: Titin-cap (Tcap) is a direct clock-controlled gene that exhibits time-of-day variations in protein amount with highest levels during the active phase.
source: Previous studies have identified titin-cap (Tcap) as a direct clock-controlled gene that exhibits time-of-day variations in protein amount with highest levels during the active phase (Gregorio et al., 1998; Hammouda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gregorio et al., 1998 and Hammouda et al., 2012.

claim: TCAP functions to anchor the titin filament at the Z-line by binding titin's Z1Z2 domain.
source: TCAP functions to anchor the titin filament at the Z-line by binding titin's Z1Z2 domain (Lee et al., 2006; Gregorio et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lee et al., 2006 and Gregorio et al., 1998.

claim: Titin protein could be exchanged daily, likely in sync with times at which TCAP protein is lowest.
source: These observations suggest a model in which titin protein could be exchanged daily, likely in sync with times at which TCAP protein is lowest.
evidence: This is speculation based on the circadian regulation of TCAP.

claim: Daily titin replacement could lead to a vulnerable period for skeletal muscle damage when TCAP is low and titin is being replaced.
source: Further, this daily replacement could lead to a vulnerable period for skeletal muscle damage (i.e., when TCAP is low and titin is being replaced).
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model of daily titin exchange.

claim: Muscle creatine kinase and leukocyte infiltration increased more substantially following evening exertion compared to morning exertion in athletes.
source: In these studies, muscle creatine kinase (Hammouda et al., 2012) and leukocyte infiltration (Hammouda et al., 2011) increased more substantially following evening exertion compared to morning exertion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hammouda et al., 2012 and Hammouda et al., 2011.
